To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the rate of loss of energy reserves during the dry period was greater for cows that developed reproductive tract disorders than for cows that remained healthy.

cows which developed a reproductive tract infection in the first 21 days of lactation, had a significantly greater loss of body condition and weight and experienced a greater rate of decline in body energy content in late gestation compared with healthy cows.

cows which developed a reproductive tract disease in the first 3 months of lactation had a significantly greater loss of energy content and body condition score in the preceding dry and early lactation period than cows that remained healthy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods for the prediction of production disease in the transition period of dairy cattle.
the development of new indicators to predict future disease risk in dairy cows.
the identification of candidate indicators of production disease in the transition period and the development of new models for the prediction and management of disease risk in early lactation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the rate of change in energy reserves in the first 15 d of the dry period is a useful indicator of the risk of developing reproductive disorders in early lactation and that cows which develop subclinical mastitis are likely to have been more productive in the previous lactations.

cows which develop a reproductive tract disorder during the first 30-days of lactation experience a greater loss in body condition in the dry period than healthy animals and cows that develop metabolic disease.

cows which develop metabolic disorders in the first 60 days of lactation experience greater loss in body condition score, body energy content and body weight in the preceding lactation and dry off period.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

body energy content in dry cows is an important indicator of disease status in early lactation, but that the rate of change of body energy content in late gestation is a better indicator than absolute body energy content.

cows that develop metabolic diseases in early lactation have significantly higher milk production at dry off in their previous lactation and a significantly higher yield:body energy content ratio at that time.

the rate of change in energy reserves during the dry period and the yield to body energy ratio in the lactation prior to calving are candidate traits to identify cows at increased risk of developing production diseases post-calving.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dry off period should be viewed as a time of transition from gestation and that monitoring of body condition and energy reserves should be a key component of dry off management.
body energy content in late gestation is a good indicator of disease risk in early lactation, particularly for reproductive tract disorders.
body energy reserves are important in the dry period for future health and productivity.
